newsitem.title: USA: UK's FOA crafts agreement to cover netting risk.
newsitem.headline: UK's FOA crafts agreement to cover netting risk.

text.p: The U.K. Futures and Options Association (FOA) said on Thursday it had almost completed an agreement that would cover firms "netting risk" in exchange-traded transactions as required by new financial rules set out by regulators in Britain.

"We believe that completion of this project will address the new requirements in a cost-effective manner...," Anthony Belchambers, chief executive of the FOA, said in a news release at a derivatives conference here.
Use of the "FOA Master Netting Agreement...will enable participating firms to secure the significant benefit of a lower capital requirement based on their net positions", he said.

The FOA is a London-based trade association for companies involved in futures, options and derivatives trading. It expects to circulate the Master Netting Agreement with the support of 25 to 30 legal opinions by the end of March.
Netting is the amalgamation of financial obligations between two or more parties -- a broker and a customer, for example -- into a single net amount.
For example, after various trades a customer owes its broker $15,000 and the broker owes the customer $10,000. The net amount outstanding is $5,000 owed to the broker.

Belchambers said in an interview there is always a risk that if a customer defaults, its liquidators could "cherry pick" the trades, claiming only the profitable transactions and leaving the broker with the losing trades.

The U.K. Securities and Futures Authority (SFA), one of Britain's main regulators, recently introduced rules that say in order for a company to have capital adequacy based on a net trading position, it must get a legal opinion saying the netting agreement is valid and enforceable.
The FOA said firms that sign up to the Master Netting Agreement would be assured their netting agreements were determined legally valid.
The regulator would use this net amount, rather than only liabilities on one side of a transaction, to judge whether a company has enough capital to cover its trades.
"We've got the commercial risk addressed and the regulatory requirements addressed," Belchambers said.
